title: For people worried about their game being easily copied
author: clydeagain
selftext:
Not a traditional dev here, but I've seen way too many people on this sub stressing out about someone stealing their AI-assisted game idea or easily cloning their mechanics. Here is the reality check:

1. Nobody is making a 100% unique game anyway

\- 99% of games out there are mashups or direct takes on existing games. Balatro is poker + deckbuilder. Stardew is a feature-rich Harvest Moon. Hollow Knight is Metroid. Thousands of clones came after them, and none of those clones hurt the originals' success.

2. AI makes making games easy, but making GOOD games is still always going to be a difficult feat.

Yes, store fronts will be flooded with AI slop and quick clones. But a good game isn't just code and art assets, it's game feel with human touch, sound design, tight balancing, lore, and content depth.

 AI can give you a starting point, but it won't balance 150 synergizing cards or tune your combat feedback for you.

3. Use AI for massive content depth, not quick shortcuts

If you're using AI, don't just use it to make a small game faster. Use it to build twice as much content as a traditional solo dev could handle. Build thousands of items, complex skill interactions, and deep mechanics. Lazy cloners won't put in that work. If your game is easy to copy with AI, I believe it means you didn't put enough depth or heart into it in the first place.

Bottomline is that you should focus on vision, scope, and polish. A cheap knockoff will always just look like a cheap knockoff.

I'm currently making a cozy single-player RPG myself which is, of course, a mix of many other successful games out there and I'm trying to make it distinguishable by making thousands of items and feature-rich overall.

Am I going to follow through til release? Maybe, maybe not. But if I do not, I'll know the difference between me and the successful developers with vision and tenacity.

replies.author: Mother-Hedgehog-5628
replies.body:
the point people are worried about is the decomp side - essentially they have your source so they see exactly how your systems were developed and then just do a reskin of those or used as a framework to make a new game. 

Theres two different sorts of coping going on - the visual kind based on videos / information scraping where they AI tries to replicate based on knowledge (which is fine, you cant protect an idea) - the other sort is the decomp side where they physically rip your game apart and steal exactly what makes it tick (basically all your intellectual property) - once they have all of that its very easy to rehash the full system into something close but rebuilt (which is what everyone is worrying about).

replies.author: Aineisa
replies.body:
Yes but this is different. You can’t upload cracked games to steam. 

You can decompile games and upload to steam while claiming it as your own. Steam currently doesn’t have a system for dealing with that. It’s why other games are delaying or cancelling demos. 

The only saving grace currently is that steam has a crazy backlog of KYC requests and game build verification which means any decompiled game uploads will take time to be published.

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
>You can’t upload cracked games to steam.

Of course you can. It's against the rules, but you can definitely do it. Your cracked game will be removed once someone notices, and you'll be banned from the service for trying, but you can do it. Steampipe accepts compiled game builds, and there's no requirement to provide source code or demonstrate that you authored the executable.

Decompilation isn't a prerequisite for redistributing stolen software, and it isn't something that suddenly became possible overnight due to AI. This is the existing piracy problem wearing new clothes, nothing more.

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
The terminology doesn't matter at all. What matters is the premise, namely that decompilation and then uploading represents a new kind of theft that wasn't previously possible. It doesn't.

Someone could already steal your game, repackage it, pass it off as their own, and attempt to sell it on Steam. That's precisely why copyright enforcement and takedown procedures exist. Uploading someone else's work was already possible.

replies.author: FallenWyvern
replies.body: Uploading it before they've finished it was rarer. It's less so now.

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
I've seen no evidence of that, nor would it be material if that were even true: It's not a new problem. It isn't enabled by this tech. There isn't more of a concern of it because of AI.

If anything, I think there's actually less of of a concern — people don't need to decomp projects anymore to figure out how they work. They can just prompt a model to generate similar aesthetics and gameplay. The value of a specific work itself is in abstract now inherently worth less to steal.

replies.author: FallenWyvern
replies.body:
"There isn't more of a concern of it because of AI"

The speed and scale of the operations of AI is what's changed. Decompiling games (or copying them) was possible before, but it took a long time and lots of effort. We can do it in a few hours now. That's the difference and to pretend like AI didn't change this is just silly.

  
I'm not saying it's more or less of a concern, but OP is concerned about it and regardless of your or my opinion on the relevancy, their concerns are valid.

replies.author: FailedGradAdmissions
replies.body:
You won’t like this, and it’ll make it way more difficult and less scalable. But if you absolutely do not want your game to be decompiled, make your own engine in a compiled language. Yeah that means no C#, no JS (no three.js), no Python.

It won’t be impossible to decompile, but it would be exponentially more difficult, your binaries will only have static assembly files and your sprites. Someone “decompiling” a game like that won’t be any different than just extracting your assets and doing a clean room new implementation of your game.

Basically if you use a low level language they can still copy your game and upload it everywhere, but they would have to basically recreate it from scratch. It’s far more likely they’ll just pirate your game and distribute it, but that’s nothing new, it’s been a thing for the last 20 years.

comments.author: EvidenceMinute4913
comments.body:
Yeah, I believe it. I’m working on an RTS game myself. The initial prototype was quick and easy, just a couple of days. Turning that into an actual full-fledged polished product is a whole different story. 

Getting the game’s architecture, design, systems, and performance where it needs to be in order to scale up took weeks of profiling and directed sessions. Getting all of the major and minor systems in place and proven to work took weeks. Polishing all the rough edges took weeks. Setting up the pipelines and tools for content took a week. And now adding all the artwork is going to take weeks, or possibly months. Then comes the balancing! 

I can imagine small mobile games with easily reproducible mechanics are easy to copy. But making anything more complex takes a ton of work. The AI speeds up development massively, yes, but it’s still development lol.

replies.author: clydeagain
replies.body: 100%! Hope you follow through all the way knowing that each milestone you noted that takes weeks would actually take usual game devs months and hope you give it all of the passion and effort to your game. It will show when the game is played.

comments.author: lucianw
comments.body:
\> Nobody is making a 100% unique game anyway

That's not really the whole story, though.

Say I have an original idea. It takes me a month of balancing, tweaking, evolving, experimenting, until I get something that's workable as a game mechanic. And I build a game with it.

Now it takes someone else with an AI just half an afternoon to reach where I was. They'll have that much more time to spend on all the other parts of the game, so that their end product will be better than mine even though they put less effort into their game.

End result: there's less incentive for me to do the experimenting phase of work.



In other walks of life we have patents to ensure that the experimenting phase still happens. In games there was a higher barrier to entry, so there wasn't as stark a discrepancy between my effort and theirs.



\> I'm currently making a cozy single-player RPG myself which is, of course, a mix of many other successful games out there and I'm trying to make it distinguishable by making thousands of items and feature-rich overall.

I think you've tuned your argument to your specific use-case, not to games development in general.

comments.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
comments.body:
RE: Copying / Cloning - Some history that applies here:

"Copying" and "Cloning" are lazy words, and its use is almost always derogatory. Want to hear something COMICAL?

Recently, people have been complaining about others "cloning" Photoshop as well as games. But here's a little history lesson.

Dan Silva was the original programmer and primary creator of Deluxe Paint for the Amiga. He developed its revolutionary brush system, including the ability to pick up, manipulate, and stamp brushes onto a canvas.

Fast-forward, and Dan Silva goes to work for Adobe. Yes, THAT Adobe. The very same Adobe that would go on to incorporate brush-stamping functionality and other concepts already popularized by Deluxe Paint on the Amiga years earlier.

So, by the logic some people are using today, Adobe and Dan Silva "COPIED" and "CLONED" Deluxe Paint. Yet somehow, the uninformed are quick to accuse others of copying or cloning Adobe.

The truth is, nearly anyone making a game today is using mechanics, concepts, and gameplay elements that existed in other games long before they ever incorporated them into their own. That's how game development has always worked. So the real question becomes, "who is copying who?"
